task.title: Hosted Workbook board for invited people who have no repository access
task.description:
Workbook reaches only people who can push to the repository. The CLI, Workbench and `workbook serve` all work from a checkout, and the board `workbook serve` shows has no sign-in. A client PM who should read and edit stories but never touch the code has no way in.

This story is a companion app, built the way Workbench was, that someone deploys to a host. It wraps Workbook, puts sign-in in front of the board, and lets invited people work on tasks from a browser with no Git account, checkout, or install.

It is optional. The CLI, Workbench and agents keep working exactly as they do today with no hosted app running, and a team that never deploys one loses nothing.

## How it fits together

- **A companion app, not a new Workbook.** Like Workbench it lives in this repository in its own directory, ships the CLI built from the same checkout, and is released on its own line. It handles sign-in, invites, accounts and serving the board. Every read and edit still goes through Workbook, so a change made by an invited person is an ordinary Workbook operation in the same versioned format the CLI writes. The app keeps no task state of its own; its copy of the tasks can be deleted and rebuilt from the repository.
- **It works against a tasks-only repository.** The deployment is pointed at a repository that holds the project's Workbook refs and no source code, and is given a credential for that repository alone. It never holds a credential for the code repository, so breaking into the server exposes tasks and nothing else. Contributors' code checkouts exchange tasks with that repository as a named remote, which is what "Support multiple task remotes" provides and why this story depends on it.
- **Invites create accounts.** The person who deploys it is its admin. The admin invites people by email; an invited person accepts by signing in, which creates their account. Only people with an account can see or change anything. The admin can revoke an account, and that takes effect at once.
- **The deployer brings the sign-in provider.** The app speaks a standard sign-in protocol and is configured with whatever provider the deployer already has. The Workbook project registers nothing with any provider and runs no service of its own.
- **Everyone invited has full access to the board.** They see every task, comment, attachment and history entry, and can create and edit tasks. Hiding some tasks from some people is out of scope for this version.

## What makes this more than a login page in front of `workbook serve`

- **The board writes as one person today.** `workbook serve` stamps every edit with the single Git `user.email` of the checkout it runs in. On a shared server each edit has to be recorded as the signed-in person, so Workbook needs a way for the companion app, and nothing else, to say who is acting on each request. The invited email is that identity: it is what appears on their edits and assignments.
- **This changes a recorded decision.** `docs/architecture.md` says there is no roster and no verification, because push access is trust. A hosted deployment adds a roster and vouches for the people on it. Push access to the tasks repository is still trust: anyone who has it can write tasks directly, and the server's rules do not bind them. The architecture document has to say both.
- **A contributor is one person in two places.** Their account email on the server has to match the `user.email` in their checkout. Otherwise Workbook treats them as two people, and a task they claimed from the CLI looks like someone else's on the board.
- **Accounts are the first Workbook data that cannot be rebuilt from Git.** Invites, accounts and sessions need durable storage and a backup, kept apart from the disposable task projection. Many hosts wipe a service's disk on every restart, so this cannot default to a file beside the checkout.
- **A saved edit must survive a restart.** With a watcher running, a write today is durable locally and published a moment later. On a host that wipes its disk, an edit that was confirmed but not yet pushed would vanish. The hosted app confirms an edit only once it cannot be lost.
- **It needs a real machine.** Workbook runs `git`, keeps a clone and a projection on disk, and synchronizes from a long-running process. A host that runs containers fits. Function-style hosts such as Vercel and Cloudflare Workers do not fit as they stand, so the earlier idea of targeting them is dropped unless a later story removes those needs.
- **The board has never faced the internet or a second user.** Its protections were built for a board on one machine used by one trusted person. Before this ships, review what changes when strangers can reach it and when one person's text is shown in another person's signed-in browser: session handling, cross-site requests, how task text and attachments are rendered and served, upload and request limits, and repeated sign-in attempts.
- **A repository with nothing but Workbook refs.** Setup and every command the server runs must work in a repository that has no branches and no code. Confirm that, and fix whatever assumes otherwise.

## What this needs from "Support multiple task remotes"

- A checkout can share its tasks through a remote other than `origin`.
- A repository holding only Workbook refs is a supported remote.

## Decisions to settle before building

Settle these first and record the outcome on this task; each one that turns into real work becomes its own task depending on this one.

1. What it is built in and what it is called. Workbench is the desktop app's name; this needs its own.
2. How the companion app sits in front of Workbook: a proxy in front of a `workbook serve` it starts, as Workbench runs one per project, or something closer. Either way, how Workbook learns who is acting, and what stops anything but the companion app from telling it.
3. Sign-in: which protocol the first version speaks, whether an emailed sign-in link is also offered for people with no provider account, and whether the email the provider reports must match the invited one.
4. How the first admin is established on a fresh deployment, and whether there can be more than one.
5. What an invited member may change. Proposed: everything about tasks; changes to statuses, priorities and keys stay with the admin.
6. Where accounts are stored, and what the deployer has to provide for it.
7. One project per deployment or several. Proposed: one, which also keeps different clients' projects on different servers.
8. Which credential the server holds for the tasks-only repository, and how it is supplied and rotated.
9. What is shipped. Proposed: a container image plus written, tested instructions for one or two container hosts, Render first since the site already deploys there.
10. Whether an operation shows that a server vouched for its author, and how.

## Done when

- Following only the published instructions, a person deploys the app to a named host, configures a sign-in provider they already have, and becomes its admin. Nobody on the Workbook project registers or runs anything for them.
- The admin invites someone who has no access to any repository. That person signs in, sees the board, creates a task and changes another's status, and a contributor's next `workbook list` in a code checkout shows both under the invited person's email.
- A change made from the CLI shows up on the hosted board without a restart.
- Someone who was never invited, or whose account was revoked, gets no board and no task data from any address the server answers on.
- The credential the server holds cannot read or write the code repository.
- After the service restarts on a host that wipes its disk, accounts and invites are intact, the board is rebuilt from the tasks-only repository, and no edit the server confirmed is missing.
- An edit made on the hosted board and a different edit to the same field made from the CLI at the same time both survive as a visible conflict, as they do between two checkouts today.
- The README has a deployment guide, and `docs/architecture.md` describes the roster, what the server vouches for, and what push access still decides.
